title: ‘Cancer is tripling and will keep increasing’: first African to lead global action against disease ready for battle
content: W hen Dr Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu last saw Gloria in Abuja, the young breast cancer patient was so ill that she was in hospital. The cancer had spread to her bones and lungs, and she was struggling with complications from the disease. Then, at a global conference on cancer thousands of miles away in Hong Kong last month, Bagudu saw her again. Gloria was walking with a stick because of the cancer in her hips, but she was attending sessions, speaking about her experience and advocating for other patients. “I saw her hopping on the corridor here. I was shocked,” Bagudu recalled. Bagudu was recounting this story on the sidelines of the World Cancer Congress in Hong Kong , attended by more than 2,000 people from 124 countries. A Nigerian paediatrician and advocate for cancer patients, Bagudu is president-elect of the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) – the first African to lead the organisation. She takes up the role as cancer cases and deaths are projected to rise sharply, with the greatest increases expected in poorer countries. “The fact that it [the election of a black person] took so long is a reflection of the inadequacy of cancer care along the entire spectrum in Africa and other low- and middle-income countries,” Bagudu says. Her election comes as countries across the global south face a growing cancer burden while also struggling with shortages of diagnostic equipment, medicines, radiotherapy services, trained specialists and financing. According to the most recent figures from the World Health Organization’s International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC), 20.6 million people were diagnosed with cancer and 9.8 million died from the disease in 2024. The IARC forecasts an annual rise in cases of 67% to more than 34m by 2050 , while deaths could reach 17.5 million, an increase of 79%. Most of the additional deaths are expected to occur in low-income countries. According to Bagudu, the forecasts reinforce the need to reorientate global cancer policy towards countries where health systems are already under pressure. “Cancer is tripling and is going to keep on increasing, and the people affected by it most are those from the global south,” she says. Her ambition is to use the UICC, which represents more than 1,100 member organisations across more than 170 countries, as a bridge between countries with limited cancer services and the research, technology and treatments being developed elsewhere. “I have this opportunity to be able to bring forth a lot of the problems that the low- and middle-income countries are facing to the global north,” she says. But Bagudu says access to cancer care cannot be solved simply by building more specialist hospitals. “We keep building cancer centres and we keep seeing that it’s not enough,” she says. Cancer centres need to be supported by screening, early diagnosis, radiotherapy, medicines, trained health workers and systems that prevent families from being pushed into financial hardship by treatment, she says. “I’m trying to reduce financial toxicity for the woman in the village,” she says. That gap is already visible in basic cancer services. UICC chief executive Cary Adams told delegates that less than half of the world’s population has access to diagnostic services, while many patients in low- and middle-income countries pay for care out of pocket. Only 14% of the estimated 73 million people who need palliative care each year have access to it, according to figures presented at the congress. Bagudu’s own work in Nigeria has focused on some of these gaps. A paediatrician and founder of the Medicaid Cancer Foundation, she helped establish Kebbi state’s first cancer-control plan and registry during her time as first lady of the Nigerian state from 2015 to 2023. Her foundation has also worked on cancer awareness and access to treatment for vulnerable patients. She has campaigned for cervical cancer prevention, including the introduction of the single-dose HPV vaccine into Nigeria’s routine immunisation programme in 2023. In 2024, she became senior adviser to Nigeria’s coordinating minister of health and social welfare with a brief that included women’s health and cancer advocacy. Bagudu now wants to take some of those lessons to the international level, including pushing for new approaches to cancer financing. She says cancer has never received the kind of global treatment financing mechanism that HIV, tuberculosis and malaria have benefited from. “Cancer has never directly been a beneficiary of global funding for treatment,” she says. She will support efforts to develop a global cancer financing platform modelled partly on the Global Fund to Fight Aids, Tuberculosis and Malaria , to mobilise resources from governments, donors and other sources to strengthen cancer prevention, diagnosis and treatment. The proposal comes as African governments face competing demands on health budgets, and international development financing is under pressure with significant cuts to foreign aid . Bagudu also wants greater attention paid to cancers that can be prevented or reduced through interventions already available. She plans to focus particularly on childhood cancers and liver cancer linked to hepatitis. That prevention must go alongside investment in diagnosis and treatment, particularly as cancer risk is shaped by factors including tobacco use, infections, alcohol, diet and obesity, she adds. She wants Africa to have a greater role in cancer research, rather than remaining primarily a recipient of discoveries and training from richer countries. “Research is a little bit more difficult because you have to have the human capacity, you have to have the interest and then you have to have the right environment,” she says. She points to emerging research centres in Nigeria, Rwanda and Kenya, as well as training programmes that bring African health workers to countries including China to develop skills in radiation therapy, cancer technology and other specialist areas. The UICC has set targets including reducing cancer mortality by 25% by 2035, reducing exposure to major cancer risk factors by 30% and ensuring that 60% of cancers are diagnosed at an early stage. Bagudu says the ultimate test of her presidency will be whether the global commitments made in conference rooms reach people far beyond them.
ranking_reason: The election of Dr. Zainab Shinkafi-Bagudu as the first African to lead the Union for International Cancer Control (UICC) highlights the growing cancer burden in low- and middle-income countries and the need for global action to address this issue.

title: Pneumonic plague, by the numbers
content: The World Health Organization said Wednesday that it had few clear answers about the recent death of a worker at a Russian institute that researched plague. The death, the subsequent isolation of hundreds of co-workers and close contacts, and reports that another worker may have pneumonia have fueled global concern about a rare form of plague. Here’s what we know about pneumonic plague by the numbers. One person who worked at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia in southeast Russia has died. There have also been media reports that a second employee of the lab has pneumonia of “undetermined cause,” the director-general of the World Health Organization said Wednesday. The 28-year-old who died was identified by the independent regional news outlet Lyudi Baikala as Darya Shipilova. Shipilova first went to the hospital September 29 in Shelekhov, a town 12 miles southwest of Irkutsk, where she worked. Three days later, on October 2 , she died. Rospotrebnadzor, the Russian agency that handles infectious disease, says the worker died of pneumonia of “unknown” origin and downplayed suspicions that her death was related to her work. WHO said it has seen local media reports about an incident in the lab involving a broken test tube. Currently, “I know what you know from the media of the test tube breaking and exposure,” Dr. Maria Van Kerkhove, director of WHO’s department of Epidemic and Pandemic Management, said Wednesday. On October 2 , the Russian government held a meeting “because they suspected a resident of the Irkutsk Institute had contracted a dangerous infection,” WHO Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said Wednesday. WHO said it first heard about the patient because it uses AI to monitor local news reports for illnesses of concern. Under international law, Russia should have reported the incident within 24 hours . After the WHO sought more information about the death, the Russian Federation replied Tuesday to say that “ no case of plague had recently been reported.” The Russian government also said it placed about 200 people who’d had contact with the worker in quarantine or under close follow-up , WHO said. WHO said it had requested further information from the government, but has not received it. “We don’t have the full picture of this event, and we are not able to conduct a full risk assessment,” Tedros said. “Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks.” A number of hospitals in the area have restricted visitors and are conducting comprehensive health checks, including requiring people to fill out questionnaires about “plague” and other infectious disease symptoms. Rospotrebnadzor, however, reassured people in the region where the lab operates that the “epidemiological situation” is stable. About 95 people work at the Anti-Plague Institute. The institute opened in 1934 to research plague. The bacterium that causes plague, Yersinia pestis, still circulates among wildlife in Siberia and neighboring regions. Globally, more than 200 kinds of mammals, mostly rodents, can contract Y. pestis, studies show . Marmots are the most common carriers in Siberia. WHO’s early assessment, based on reports that the cause of death was pneumonic plague, was that the risk to the general public appeared to be low. There are thousands of suspected plague cases around the world every year, Van Kerkhove said. From 2019 to 2025, 10 countries reported almost 4,000 suspected human plague cases and 423 deaths , WHO said Wednesday. Central Asia has the largest number of foci, or areas where the disease is present. People are most often infected after exposure to infected rodents. There are four major types of plague caused by Y. pestis that attack different parts of the body: WHO said it conducted an initial assessment of risk based on an understanding that the Russian lab worker’s case could be pneumonic plague. Pneumonic plague is the only form of the bacterial infection that can spread from person to person. The basic reproduction number is about 1.1 to 1.3 , meaning that one person with pneumonic plague can spread the disease through a cough or sneeze to about 1.3 people , studies show . Droplets from infected animals can also transmit it. People can develop symptoms as soon as 24 hours after exposure, according to Dr. Rutul Dalal, an infectious disease physician at Penn State Health St. Joseph Medical Center. Typically, people with pneumonic plague are so sick that they rarely spread it because “it’s very difficult for someone to even walk, do their daily activities, let alone travel,” he said. There’s also very limited travel to the US from this area. There are no direct flights between Russia and the US, Dalal noted. A spokesperson for the US Department of Health and Human Services said about 200 travelers from the region arrive in the United States over the course of a year. “These travelers arrive at designated airports where CDC personnel are already positioned and prepared to identify potential health concerns, conduct public health assessments, and take appropriate action when warranted,” the HHS spokesperson said. By the time infected travelers reached the US, they would already be showing symptoms, Dalal said. “Of course, you have to be careful,” he said, because “the world is a little village now,” as everyone learned during the Covid-19 pandemic. Patients treated within the first 24 hours of infection have the best chance of surviving. People with plague typically get at least 10 to 14 days of antibiotics. Five antibiotics typically work best against plague: ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin, moxifloxacin, gentamicin and streptomycin. Doctors have used plague vaccines since the 19th century , but it’s not clear how protective they are against pneumonic plague. WHO doesn’t recommend vaccination except for high-risk groups and lab workers who are regularly exposed to the bacteria. The bacterium that causes plague circulates on every continent except Oceania. It has infected human populations for at least 5,000 years , studies of archaeological sites show. Three of the world’s deadliest pandemics were caused by Y. pestis. 1924 was the year of the last documented person-to-person transmission of pneumonic plague in the US, during an outbreak in Los Angeles. Since the 1990s, most human cases have been in Africa, according to WHO . July 2025 was when the last person in the US died from pneumonic plague. The person lived in Arizona and was probably infected while working with sick cats. In the US about five human cases are reported every year.
ranking_reason: This event highlights the potential risks of laboratory accidents and the importance of transparency in reporting public health incidents.
